'''Ruth Margaret Williams''' (born 1945) is a British mathematician at the [[University of Cambridge]]. Her research focuses on discrete gravity.

==Early life and education==
Williams was born in [[Birmingham]] and attended primary schools in [[Lozells]] and Banners Gate. Her secondary education was at Sutton Coldfield High School for Girls. The first member of her family to go to university, she read mathematics at [[Girton College, Cambridge]], then moved to [[Imperial College, London]], for her PhD, which was in [[theoretical physics]] and focused on current algebras. She obtained a postdoctoral research position at the [[Center for Theoretical Studies, University of Miami|Center for Theoretical Studies at the University of Miami]] (1968-1970). She held a research position at [[Imperial College]] (1970-1973) and a temporary lectureship at the [[University of Bristol]] (1973-1974), before moving back to a [[Hertha Ayrton]] Research Fellowship at [[Girton College]] in 1974.<ref name="DAMPT">{{cite web |title= DAMPT homepage|url=http://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/person/rmw7|website=University of Cambridge|accessdate=12 August 2020}}></ref>

==Career==
In 1976, Williams became an Official Fellow, Lecturer and Director of Studies in Mathematics at [[Girton College]],<ref name="DAMPT"/> positions she held until she retired in 2012. At the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, [[University of Cambridge]], she was a temporary lecturer (1991-1994),<ref name="DAMPT"/> Assistant Director of Research (1994-2002)<ref name="DAMPT"/> and Reader in Mathematical Physics<ref name="DAMPT"/> from 2002 until retiring in 2012. She is now a Life Fellow at [[Girton College]].<ref>{{cite web |title= Girton Life Fellows|url=https://www.girton.cam.ac.uk/prospective-students/subjects/economics/fellows-and-teaching-officers-in-economics/|website=Girton College, University of Cambridge|accessdate=12 August 2020}}</ref> Throughout her time in Cambridge, she lectured on and supervised most of the courses in theoretical physics.

==Research==
Williams’ early research was in [[elementary particle physics]], then during her second postdoctoral position she started working in classical [[general relativity]]. Eventually, she combined these two interests by working in [[quantum gravity]] in an attempt to find a unified theory of [[quantum mechanics]] and [[general relativity]]. Her particular approach, called [[Regge calculus]], is a version of discrete gravity where curved space-times are approximated by collections of flat simplices. This may be thought of as a generalisation of [[geodesic domes]] to higher dimensions. Williams’ work on Regge calculus includes the classical evolution of model universes,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=P. A. |last2=Williams |first2=Ruth M. |year=1973 |title=Dynamics of the Friedmann Universe Using Regge Calculus |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.7.965 |journal=[[Physical Review D]] |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=965–971 |bibcode=1973PhRvD...7..965C |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.7.965 |accessdate=22 July 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and numerical simulations of discrete quantum gravity,<ref>{{cite journal |title=Simplicial quantum gravity with higher derivative terms: Formalism and numerical results in four dimensions |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0550-3213%2886%2990518-3 |journal= Nuclear Physics B|year=1986 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(86)90518-3 |accessdate=22 July 2020|last1=Hamber |first1=Herbert W. |last2=Williams |first2=Ruth M. |volume=269 |issue=3–4 |pages=712–743 |bibcode=1986NuPhB.269..712H |url-access=subscription }}</ref> together with investigations of the relationship between Regge calculus and the [[continuum theory]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Quantum Regge Calculus |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693%2881%2990848-0|journal=Physics Letters B|year=1981 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(81)90848-0 |accessdate=22 July 2020|last1=Roček |first1=M. |last2=Williams |first2=Ruth M. |volume=104 |issue=1 |pages=31–37 |bibcode=1981PhLB..104...31R |url-access=subscription }}</ref> She has written around 100 papers on her research.<ref>{{cite web |title=Article List |url=https://arxiv.org/find/gr-qc/1/au:+Williams_Ruth_M/0/1/0/all/0/1|website=arXiv.org|accessdate=22 July 2020}}</ref>

==Knowledge transfer==
Williams has given talks on her research to student societies, sixth formers and younger pupils. She has been Treasurer of the Cambridgeshire branch of the [[Royal Institution]] Mathematics Workshops, which runs Saturday morning sessions to foster the mathematical interest of local twelve- and thirteen-year-olds.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cambridge Branch of the Ri Mathematics Masterclasses |url=https://www.ri-masterclass-cambs.org/aboutus/ |website=The Royal Institution|accessdate=12 August 2020}}</ref>

===Non-technical articles===
Article in ''[[New Scientist]]'': ''Building blocks for space and time''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Building blocks for space and time |journal=New Scientist |date=12 June 1986 |issue=110 |pages=48–51}}</ref>

==Women in STEM==
Williams has always been especially concerned that women should not be deterred from reaching their potential as mathematicians. To this end, and encouraged by [[Dusa McDuff]], she started the British Women in Mathematics Day, which is now an annual event.<ref>{{cite web |title=Women in mathematics |url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/events/women-mathematics-day |website=[[London Mathematical Society]] |accessdate=22 July 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Williams is the widow of Czech-born British mathematician, [[Jan Saxl]], Professor of Algebra at the University of Cambridge, and they have one daughter, Miriam.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Professor Jan Saxl|url=https://www.cai.cam.ac.uk/news/professor-jan-saxl|access-date=2020-08-08|website=Gonville & Caius}}</ref>
